evals.prompt: Score this deal for me. Halberd Freight, 240-seat rollout of our TMS, $195K ACV, six people involved on their side, they have formal procurement plus a SOC 2 review to get through, we're at proposal. Metrics: about $600K a year saved on empty miles, I built the model off their volumes. EB is the COO, my contact says he's fully behind it. Criteria: their RFP lists 14 requirements. Process: they told me they want it signed by end of Q3. Paper: procurement there is a rubber stamp, my contact has done it before. Pain: their dispatchers hate the tool they've got. Champion: the ops manager loves us, we talk every week. Competition: nobody else is in it. I've got it at 19 out of 24, does that look right?
evals.expected_output: An eight-element scorecard in which every claim lacking a buyer-side artefact is knocked down to 1, the self-scored 19/24 is rejected, the Champion gate caps the verdict at Under-qualified, each knocked-down score appears under Challenged with its reason, and the top next action is a buyer-visible test.
expectations: Scores all eight elements, since the deal is $195K with six stakeholders and a formal procurement and security path.
Scores Metrics 1, on the ground that the savings figure is a rep-built model the buyer never confirmed.
Scores Economic Buyer 1 or 0, treating 'my contact says he's fully behind it' as hearsay rather than the Access rung, since no introduction has been committed.
Scores Decision Criteria 1, on the ground that an RFP requirement sheet is not buyer-confirmed decision criteria.
Scores Decision Process 1, on the ground that the end-of-Q3 date is not a buyer-owned decision process.
Scores Paper Process 1, on the ground that 'procurement is a rubber stamp' names no mapped path, no owners, and no timelines.
Scores Implicate the Pain no higher than 2, because the dispatcher complaint carries no costed consequence.
Scores Champion 1, identifying the ops manager as a coach who has not acted.
Scores Competition 1, noting that do-nothing or inertia has not been examined.
Rejects the self-scored 19/24 and reports a materially lower total.
States that the Champion gate caps the verdict at Under-qualified regardless of the total.
Includes a Challenged section listing each knocked-down score together with the missing artefact as the reason.
The single top next action is an ask the buyer either performs or refuses, not rep-side work such as updating the CRM or building a deck.

evals.prompt: Quick one. $11K a year, it's a solo founder, he's the only person involved, no procurement, no legal team, no security review. He told me on Friday he'd sign this month. Run MEDDPICC on it and tell me if it's real.
evals.expected_output: A right-sized scorecard covering only the letters that survive for a deal this size, with Economic Buyer folded into Champion, a shrunken denominator, and no next action attached to any dropped element.
expectations: Right-sizes the element list before scoring instead of scoring all eight elements.
Scores only Metrics, Implicate the Pain, and Champion, adding Decision Process solely if a multi-step approval is reported.
States that Economic Buyer and Champion collapse into the same person on this deal and scores them as one letter rather than dropping Economic Buyer outright.
Explicitly drops Paper Process, Decision Criteria, and Competition from the scored list.
Uses a denominator matching the reduced element list rather than 24.
Attaches no next action to any element that was right-sized out.
States that scoring all eight letters on a deal this size would be process theatre or over-engineering.
Treats the 'he'd sign this month' date as rep-reported rather than buyer-owned evidence of a decision process.
Confirms the element list with the user before scoring, or states the right-sizing decision and its reason explicitly in the output.
States the definitions used for the second C and for Pain, and that weighting is equal by default.
Presents disqualification or a low band as a legitimate outcome rather than forcing a path forward.

evals.prompt: I run a 14-rep team at Corvid Analytics, $2.1M quarterly quota, our forecast accuracy is sitting around 55%. I'm rolling deal scoring out across the team before next quarter. Build me the rubric the reps will score their opportunities on, and the slide that tells my VP what we should expect to get out of it.
evals.expected_output: An evidence-based 0-3 rubric with equal weighting stated, plus an expectations slide that quarantines unreplicated vendor outcome figures, labels any vendor number it does quote, and points at the one measure that can falsify the rubric.
expectations: Defines the scoring ladder as 0 unknown, 1 assumed, 2 stated, 3 validated, with 2 meaning the buyer said it and 3 meaning the buyer demonstrated it.
States that the axis is evidence rather than presence: a letter scores on what the buyer did, not on what the rep can name.
States that weighting is equal by default and that per-letter weighting is practice-dependent rather than canonical.
Does not present '18% higher win rates', '24% larger deals', or '26% shorter sales cycles' as expected outcomes.
Does not promise a forecast-accuracy figure such as 95%.
Does not cite 'increase deal size by 62%' or 'double your win rate' as an expected result.
Does not cite '40% higher close rates', '78% of accounts are single-threaded', or a 2.4x or 3.1x multi-threading multiplier.
Labels any vendor-published figure it does quote as a vendor claim rather than an independent measurement.
Attributes the 60% lost-to-inertia figure to the methodology publisher's own claim if it cites it at all.
Describes any Ebsta or Pavilion benchmark figure it cites as a relative lift rather than a point difference.
Warns that scorecards getting filled while forecast accuracy stays flat means the evidence definitions are too loose.
Names band versus realized outcome as the measure that can falsify the rubric, and notes it only pays out after a full quarter of closed deals.
Distinguishes rules published by the methodology from rules this scorecard sets itself.

evals.prompt: Deal's already scored, I just need to know what to chase. Wexler Industrial, $120K ACV, seven stakeholders, they have procurement but we're nowhere near a yes yet, mid-cycle. Scores: Metrics 1, Economic Buyer 1 (I know the CFO's name, no intro on the table), Decision Criteria 1, Decision Process 2, Paper Process 1, Pain 2, Champion 3 because he's presented us internally twice and sent me their scoring sheet, Competition 1. Forecast call is Friday. One thing though: I've already burned a lot of goodwill with my champion getting the security questionnaire answered, so I'm not asking him for anything that costs him internally. What do I go do?
evals.expected_output: A ranked ask list in which the effort ceiling deletes the Economic Buyer meeting and the procurement introduction outright, the Friday checkpoint demotes the slow asks, and the recommendation is a near-zero buyer-visible ask.
expectations: Deletes the Economic Buyer meeting from the ask menu rather than ranking it last, because the stated effort ceiling forbids spending the champion's internal credit.
Deletes the procurement introduction on the same ground.
States which asks were deleted and the constraint that removed them.
Does not recommend the Economic Buyer meeting as the next action despite Economic Buyer being among the weakest-evidenced elements.
Recommends a near-zero ask that fits inside a conversation already scheduled.
Ranks the remaining asks by verdict change per unit of effort rather than by element importance.
States effort as an order of magnitude such as near-zero, an hour, or a week, never as a currency amount.
Notes that the Friday checkpoint demotes the paper-process map because it cannot land in time.
Attaches no next action to Champion, which scores 3.
Lists the starved high-value asks under a Deferred heading together with the condition that would promote them.
Applies no gate cap, since Champion is above 1 and Economic Buyer is above 0.
Keeps Economic Buyer at 1 rather than raising it on the strength of the champion's internal presentations, because no introduction has been committed.

evals.prompt: Ferrous Labs, $310K over three years, nine people involved, legal and infosec both in the loop, we're in technical validation. Honestly nobody on my side knows who actually signs. My champion is a platform director, he's presented us internally twice and sent me their scoring sheet. They emailed me that the March outage cost them $1.4M. Their target is cutting incident MTTR by 40%, that's their own number out of their board deck. Criteria are in the scoring sheet they sent. They walked me through the committee steps on a recorded call, but there's nothing written down between us. Nobody has mentioned procurement at all. They named two rivals and said doing nothing is genuinely on the table. Score it.
evals.expected_output: An eight-element scorecard with several genuine 3s, an Economic Buyer at 0 that caps the verdict at Under-qualified regardless of the total, and the Economic Buyer meeting promoted ahead of cheaper asks on the stated gate condition.
expectations: Scores all eight elements, since the deal is $310K with nine stakeholders and legal and infosec involved.
Scores Economic Buyer 0 and states the verdict is capped at Under-qualified regardless of the total.
Does not report the band as Forecast-ready or Real but gapped despite a raw percentage in the 55-79% range.
Scores Champion 3, citing the internal presentations and the shared scoring sheet as observable acts.
Scores Metrics 3, citing the buyer-supplied MTTR target from their own board deck.
Scores Implicate the Pain 3, citing the emailed $1.4M outage cost as a costed consequence the buyer stated.
Scores Decision Process 2 rather than 3, because the steps were described but no plan was co-edited with the buyer.
Scores Competition 2 rather than 3, because alternatives were named but no win plan positions against do-nothing.
Scores Paper Process 1 or 0, since procurement has never been discussed.
Names the Economic Buyer meeting as the first action, overriding the default efficiency order.
States that the promotion condition, the gate capping the verdict, put the Economic Buyer meeting ahead of cheaper asks, rather than its value alone.
Phrases the top action as an ask the champion either performs or refuses.
Notes that a champion unwilling or unable to make the introduction would itself call the Champion score into question.

evals.prompt: I sell residential solar. Couple in their fifties, $61K system, one home visit done. The wife is keen, she's the one who called us after a neighbour's referral. The husband keeps saying the payback maths doesn't work. They'd need financing and haven't applied anywhere. They told me their power bill is $480 a month and climbing. Is this one real? Run the qualification framework over it.
evals.expected_output: A four-element household scorecard, labelled as a structural analogy, keeping the financing path in the scored set and promoting it, with the skeptical spouse identified as the money-controlling role.
expectations: States that the consumer mapping is a structural analogy rather than established practice for this methodology.
Right-sizes to roughly four elements rather than scoring all eight on a household purchase.
Keeps Paper Process in the scored set, read as the financing path.
States that Paper Process inverts the usual drop order here and is promoted by default rather than dropped first.
Maps the skeptical husband to the money-controlling, veto-holding role rather than treating the enthusiastic wife as sufficient.
Maps Champion to the household member who sells the other when the salesperson is not present.
Scores the financing element 1 or 0, since no application has been started.
Scores Metrics no higher than 2: the $480 bill is stated by the buyer but the lender's figure is unconfirmed.
Names waiting or doing nothing as the live competing alternative even if Competition is right-sized out of the scored list.
Recommends a buyer-visible test such as getting both spouses into the same conversation, or a financing application actually submitted by a stated date.
Keeps the evidence ladder, the anti-inflation rule, and the gates identical to the business-to-business version, changing only the cast.
Does not present a full eight-element scorecard as the more rigorous option for this deal.

evals.prompt: Our org runs this framework but our second C is Compelling Event, not Competition, and we weight Economic Buyer and Champion double. Score this one under our model. Nimbus Freight Systems, $140K ACV, five stakeholders, procurement is definitely involved, we're at business case. My champion is the VP Ops, she's booked me into the CFO's calendar for next Thursday. Metrics: I put $900K of avoided overtime in front of her and she said that sounds about right. Pain: she said the overtime problem cost them a customer last year but wouldn't put a figure on it. Criteria: she walked me through them on a call, nothing captured. Decision process: same, described verbally, nothing written between us. Paper: she says security review runs six weeks and legal another two, she's watched it happen twice. Compelling event: their WMS contract expires in March and they can't renew it.
evals.expected_output: A scorecard run under the team's own definitions and weighting, with the do-nothing probe deleted from the ask menu, a mostly-2 profile reflecting verbal-only evidence, and no gate cap.
expectations: Uses the team's Compelling Event as the second C instead of Competition and states that substitution in the output.
Applies the team's double weighting for Economic Buyer and Champion instead of equal weighting, and states the weighting used.
Deletes the do-nothing probe from the ask menu, since the team standard replaced Competition.
Notes the mapping between the team's definitions and this scorecard's own defaults.
Scores Economic Buyer 2, the Access rung, because the introduction is committed but the meeting is not yet held.
Scores Champion 3, citing the booked CFO introduction as the act.
Scores Metrics 2 rather than 3, because the buyer verbally agreed once to a figure the rep proposed.
Scores Implicate the Pain 2 rather than 3, because the problem is named but uncosted.
Scores Decision Criteria 2 rather than 3, because the criteria were described verbally and never captured.
Scores Decision Process 2 rather than 3, because no plan was co-edited with the buyer.
Scores Paper Process 2 rather than 3, because the path is sketched but not mapped with named owners and timelines.
Applies no gate cap, since Champion is 3 and Economic Buyer is 2.
Does not add Competition as a ninth scored letter alongside the team's Compelling Event.

evals.prompt: Already scored mine, came out 15 out of 24. Metrics 2, Economic Buyer 1, Decision Criteria 2, Decision Process 3, Paper Process 1, Pain 3, Champion 2, Competition 1. Everything I know about this account came from one guy, Dmitri, their engineering manager, great bloke, tells me everything. Give me my action list for the week.
evals.expected_output: A ratio-ordered action list with one singled-out top ask, every action phrased as a buyer-visible test, single-threading flagged, and the Decision Process 3 re-challenged against the Economic Buyer 1.
expectations: Flags single-threading, since one contact supplies the evidence for every element.
Re-challenges the Decision Process 3 against the Economic Buyer 1 as a likely inflation artifact rather than accepting both.
Attaches a next action to every element scoring below 3.
Attaches no next action to the elements scoring 3.
Phrases every action as an ask the buyer performs or refuses, never as rep-side work such as updating the CRM or drafting an internal note.
Orders the actions by verdict change per unit of effort rather than by element order or by importance.
Singles out one top action instead of handing over a flat list.
States effort per action as an order of magnitude, never as a currency amount.
Names the starved high-value asks under a Deferred heading with the condition that would promote them.
Notes that inertia is unexamined and that Competition cannot exceed 2 without a do-nothing analysis.
Reports a band of Real but gapped or lower, never Forecast-ready.
Names a re-score trigger: the event or date for the next scoring pass.

evals.prompt: Can you MEDDPICC my deal for me? It's an enterprise one, been dragging since April.
evals.expected_output: A single opening question, not a scorecard: the interview opens on deal-frame questions one at a time with multiple-choice options, and nothing is scored before the element list is confirmed.
expectations: Asks questions rather than producing a scored scorecard from the information given.
Asks one question per message rather than presenting a numbered list of questions in a single message.
Offers multiple-choice answers wherever the question admits them.
Asks deal-frame questions, such as deal type, size and stakeholder count, stage, and who set the expected close date, before any per-element evidence question.
Asks whether procurement, security review, or legal redlines are involved on the buyer's side.
Asks whether the user's team mandates its own definitions, scale, or weighting, and commits to using theirs if so.
Asks by what date the scorecard must change something.
Asks whether the user wants a one-off read or a record that compounds across reviews.
Asks what the effort ceiling is: how many buyer asks can be made and how much champion credit can be spent.
Confirms the element list with the user before scoring anything.
Invents no scores, artefacts, or buyer statements the user has not supplied.
Asks, per element, for the buyer-side artefact or event behind the claim rather than for the claim alone.

evals.prompt: Is this one real? $47K, three people on their side, mid-stage. I bumped into their finance director at a conference last month and she told me the budget's approved for this. My main contact told me over drinks that they're definitely going with us. I've got nothing in writing from them at all, every note is mine. The close date in the CRM is one I put in, next month.
evals.expected_output: A right-sized scorecard where unrecorded verbal recall scores as assumption, the Champion gate caps the verdict, the band is stated in forecast terms, and re-qualifying or disqualifying is offered as a valid outcome.
expectations: Applies the rule that evidence must exist in writing or on a recorded call, so hallway and over-drinks recollections do not count as buyer-side evidence.
Scores Economic Buyer no higher than 1 despite the reported 'budget is approved' conversation.
Scores Champion no higher than 1, since the contact's enthusiasm comes with no observable act.
Applies the Champion gate and caps the verdict at Under-qualified or lower.
Treats the close date as rep-set rather than buyer-owned and scores Decision Process accordingly.
Right-sizes this deal by dropping Paper Process, since no procurement is reported.
States that re-qualifying from discovery or disqualifying is a legitimate outcome.
Names exactly one element as the biggest gap.
Gives that gap a buyer-visible test whose refusal is itself informative.
States the band in forecast terms rather than as a grade or a mark out of ten.
Records the compelling event as honestly absent rather than manufacturing one.
Uses a denominator matching the reduced element list rather than 24.
